title: Resistance of a galvanometer by the half-deflection method, and its figure of merit
objective: To determine the resistance of a moving-coil galvanometer by the half-deflection method.
To find its figure of merit.
To calculate the current required to produce full-scale deflection.

theory.statement: In the half-deflection method a galvanometer is connected through a high resistance to a cell and the deflection noted. A shunt is then placed across the galvanometer and adjusted until the deflection falls to exactly half. Under the right conditions the shunt resistance is then equal to the galvanometer resistance.
theory.derivationNote:
With the shunt open, the current through the circuit is I = E/(R + G) and the galvanometer shows a deflection θ. When a shunt S is connected across the galvanometer, the parallel combination GS/(G + S) is very small compared with R, so the total current drawn from the cell is essentially unchanged. That total current now divides between the two parallel branches. If the deflection falls to exactly θ/2, then exactly half the current is passing through the galvanometer and half through the shunt. Equal currents in parallel branches means equal resistances, giving the familiar approximate result G = S.

That result is only as good as the assumption behind it. Working without the approximation, the condition for half deflection is S = GR/(R + G), which rearranges to the exact expression G = SR/(R − S). Because S is always slightly less than G, the crude reading G ≈ S always underestimates the galvanometer resistance, typically by a couple of per cent when R is a few thousand ohms. Making R smaller makes the error worse, which is exactly why the method demands a large series resistance.

The figure of merit is k = E/((R + G)θ), the current needed for one division of deflection. A small k means a large deflection for a small current, that is, a SENSITIVE galvanometer — the opposite of what the phrase 'figure of merit' suggests to most students. The current for full-scale deflection is then Ig = nk, where n is the number of divisions on the scale.
keyEquations: I = E/(R + G) with the shunt open
Half deflection condition: S = GR/(R + G)
Approximate result: G ≈ S, valid only when R ≫ G
Figure of merit k = E/((R + G)·θ), in ampere per division

apparatus.name: Moving-coil galvanometer
apparatus.why: The instrument whose resistance and sensitivity are being measured

apparatus.name: High resistance box
apparatus.why: Limits the current to a safe value and provides the large R the method requires

apparatus.name: Low resistance box
apparatus.spec: 0 to 500 Ω, used as the shunt
apparatus.why: Placed across the galvanometer and reduced until the deflection halves

apparatus.name: Battery or accumulator
apparatus.why: Supplies a constant emf; a fading cell would change the deflection between readings

apparatus.name: One-way keys
apparatus.why: Allow the circuit and the shunt to be closed independently

apparatus.name: Connecting wires
apparatus.why: Keep lead resistance negligible compared with R

procedure.text: Before connecting anything to the cell, set the high resistance box to a few thousand ohms. A galvanometer must never be connected straight across a cell.
Connect the cell, the key, the high resistance box and the galvanometer in series.
Close the key and adjust R until the deflection is large but still on the scale, about 20 to 25 divisions.
Note this deflection θ with the shunt still disconnected.
Connect the low resistance box across the galvanometer as a shunt.
Reduce the shunt until the deflection falls to exactly half its previous value.
Record the shunt resistance at half deflection.
Repeat the whole procedure for two or three different values of R.
Calculate G from G = SR/(R − S), and the figure of merit from k = E/((R + G)θ).

steps: Pair each open-shunt deflection with the shunted reading taken at the same R
Check that the shunted deflection really is half the open one
G = SR/(R − S) for each pair, then take the mean
Compare with the crude value G ≈ S to see the size of the approximation error
k = E/((R + G)·θ) in ampere per division
Full-scale current Ig = n·k where n is the number of divisions

expectedResult.statement: The resistance of the given galvanometer is about 60 Ω by the half-deflection method, and its figure of merit is about 26 µA per division, so a current of roughly 780 µA gives full-scale deflection. The crude reading G ≈ S underestimates the resistance by about two per cent, and that error grows if the series resistance is reduced.

safety: Never connect a galvanometer directly across a cell. Its coil takes only microamps at full scale and would burn out instantly.
Always set the high resistance box to its maximum before closing the key, then reduce it until the deflection is convenient.
Open the key between readings so the cell does not run down and the coil does not heat.
Do not exceed the scale. If the pointer slams against the end stop, open the key at once and increase R.
Handle the galvanometer gently; the suspension and pivot are delicate.
sourcesOfError: The assumption that connecting the shunt does not change the total current is only exactly true if R is infinite.
Resistance of the connecting leads and of dirty plug contacts in the resistance boxes.
The cell's emf falling slightly as current is drawn, so the open and shunted readings refer to different emfs.
Judging exactly half of the first deflection, especially if that deflection was an odd number of divisions.
Heating of the galvanometer coil, which slightly raises its resistance.
Parallax while reading the pointer against the scale.

viva.question: Why is the method called the half-deflection method?
viva.expectedConcept: Because the shunt is adjusted until the deflection falls to exactly half its original value. At that point half the current goes through the galvanometer and half through the shunt, which is what makes the two resistances comparable.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking it refers to using half the scale.

viva.question: Why does halving the deflection mean the currents are equal?
viva.expectedConcept: The deflection of a moving-coil galvanometer is proportional to the current through its coil. If the total current is essentially unchanged and the deflection halves, then the coil is carrying half of what it was, so the other half must be flowing through the shunt. Equal currents through parallel branches means equal resistances.
viva.answerLogic: Deflection ∝ current, plus the current-divider argument.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming the total current also halves.

viva.question: Why must R be much larger than G?
viva.expectedConcept: The method assumes that connecting the shunt does not change the current drawn from the cell. That current is E/(R + parallel combination), so it only stays constant if R dominates. If R is comparable with G, the total current rises noticeably when the shunt is connected and the value of G obtained is wrong.
viva.answerLogic: Identifies the assumption and what breaks it.
viva.commonMisconception: Believing R is there only to protect the galvanometer.

viva.question: Is G = S exact?
viva.expectedConcept: No. The exact condition is S = GR/(R + G), which rearranges to G = SR/(R − S). Since S is always a little less than G, taking G = S always underestimates the resistance, by about two per cent when R is a few thousand ohms.
viva.answerLogic: Knows both forms and the direction of the error.
viva.commonMisconception: Treating G = S as the true result rather than an approximation.

viva.question: What is the figure of merit of a galvanometer?
viva.expectedConcept: The current needed to produce a deflection of one division, k = E/((R + G)θ), measured in ampere per division.
viva.commonMisconception: Confusing it with the resistance or with the full-scale current.

viva.question: Does a large figure of merit mean a good galvanometer?
viva.expectedConcept: No, the opposite. A large figure of merit means a large current is needed for each division, so the instrument is insensitive. A SMALL figure of merit means a tiny current produces a big deflection, which is what makes a galvanometer useful. The name is misleading.
viva.answerLogic: Inverse relation between k and sensitivity.

viva.question: How is the current for full-scale deflection found?
viva.expectedConcept: Multiply the figure of merit by the number of divisions on the scale: Ig = nk. For a 30 division scale with k of 26 µA per division, that is about 780 µA.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the full-scale current is the same as the figure of merit.

viva.question: Why should the key be opened between readings?
viva.expectedConcept: To stop current being drawn continuously. That would run the cell down so its emf falls between readings, and it would heat the galvanometer coil and raise its resistance. Both effects make the readings inconsistent.
viva.answerLogic: Protects the cell and the coil.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking it is only to save the battery.

viva.question: What would happen if you connected the galvanometer straight to the cell?
viva.expectedConcept: With only its own tens of ohms in the circuit, a 2 V cell would drive tens of milliamps through a coil rated for a few hundred microamps. The pointer would slam against the stop and the fine coil would burn out at once.
viva.answerLogic: Quantifies why the series resistance is essential.
viva.commonMisconception: Thinking the pointer would simply go off scale harmlessly.

viva.question: Why is a moving-coil galvanometer's deflection proportional to the current?
viva.expectedConcept: The coil hangs in a radial magnetic field produced by shaped pole pieces and a soft-iron core, so the field is always parallel to the plane of the coil. The torque is then NBIA regardless of the coil's position, and it is balanced by the spring's restoring torque, which is proportional to the twist. So the deflection is proportional to the current.
viva.answerLogic: Radial field gives a position-independent torque.
viva.commonMisconception: Assuming proportionality holds for any field shape.

scientificValidation.formula: S = GR/(R + G) at half deflection; G = SR/(R − S); k = E/((R + G)·θ); Ig = n·k
assumptions: R is much larger than G, so the total current barely changes when the shunt is connected
The cell emf is steady and its internal resistance is negligible beside R
Deflection is proportional to the current through the coil
Lead and contact resistances are negligible
scientificValidation.validRange: R from 500 to 10000 Ω; shunt from 10 to 300 Ω; deflections from 5 to 30 divisions
scientificValidation.unitSystem: Resistance in ohm, current in microampere, deflection in scale divisions
edgeCases: R = 0 would destroy the galvanometer — blocked
S = R makes the exact formula divide by zero — blocked
R comparable with G makes the approximation visibly wrong — warned
An off-scale pointer yields no reading and the record is refused
A deflection below 5 divisions carries a large percentage error — warned
expectedBehaviour: The exact formula recovers the true resistance for every galvanometer in the tray
The crude form G ≈ S is low by about two per cent at R = 3000 Ω
The approximation error grows as R is reduced
Halving the deflection corresponds exactly to S = GR/(R + G)
